reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with gradual central visual loss and metamorphopsia, often first noticed as a distortion on an Amsler grid
Most cases are idiopathic and age-related, affecting women more often, and are usually unilateral at presentation
The Watzke-Allen slit-beam test and a positive scotoma to a fixation target support the diagnosis at the bedside
Optical coherence tomography is the diagnostic standard and stages the hole while distinguishing it from a pseudohole or lamellar hole
Vitreomacular traction from posterior vitreous separation is the principal mechanism in idiopathic disease
Surgical repair by vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peel and gas tamponade closes most holes, sometimes with face-down posturing
Trauma and high myopia are recognised secondary causes and myopic holes carry a higher detachment risk
Earlier and smaller holes achieve better closure rates and visual recovery than large chronic ones
reference.pathophysiology: An idiopathic full-thickness macular hole develops when tangential and anteroposterior traction from the perifoveal vitreous acts on the fovea during posterior vitreous detachment. This traction elevates and then dehisces the foveal tissue, creating a full-thickness defect with surrounding cuff of subretinal fluid and cystic change. Progressive stages run from foveal detachment and pseudocyst through to an established round hole. Secondary holes may follow blunt trauma or the mechanical stresses of high myopia, where posterior staphyloma adds traction.
additionalDifferentials: Macular pseudohole from an epiretinal membrane
Vitreomacular traction syndrome without a hole
additionalInvestigations: Optical coherence tomography to confirm and stage a full-thickness hole and measure its diameter
Amsler grid and Watzke-Allen testing to characterise the central defect
Dilated fundus examination of both eyes as the fellow eye carries some risk
Axial length or refraction assessment when myopic traction is suspected
History of ocular trauma in atypical or younger patients
redFlags: Myopic macular hole with signs of retinal detachment requiring urgent surgical assessment
Sudden worsening or new peripheral field loss suggesting an associated detachment
Bilateral or fellow-eye symptoms indicating risk to the only good eye
Traumatic hole with other posterior segment injury
reference.prognosis: Modern vitrectomy with membrane peeling closes the large majority of idiopathic holes, and visual improvement is best when the hole is small and of short duration; large, chronic, or myopic holes have lower closure rates and more limited recovery.
pitfalls: Confusing a pseudohole or lamellar hole with a full-thickness hole without OCT confirmation
Delaying referral so that a small, highly repairable hole enlarges and chronifies
Overlooking a coexisting retinal detachment in a myopic eye
Setting unrealistic expectations for visual recovery in long-standing holes
management: Vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peel and gas tamponade is the definitive treatment, closing the large majority of full-thickness holes
Post-operative prone or face-down posturing and avoidance of air travel and altitude while intraocular gas persists
Consider observation for very early vitreomacular-traction-stage holes that may resolve spontaneously, with pharmacological vitreolysis using ocriplasmin in selected traction cases
Optical coherence tomography to confirm and stage the hole and to monitor anatomical closure after surgery
Manage the cataract that commonly follows vitrectomy
Examine and monitor the fellow eye given its risk, with Amsler grid self-monitoring
Prompt referral to a vitreoretinal surgeon, as earlier repair of small, recent holes gives the best visual outcome
